quests.instruction: Before eating a banana, Emma pulls off its yellow outer layer with just her fingers. Which word names what she just did?
quests.question: Peel
quests.hint: This word describes removing a fruit's skin, not cutting its inside.
quests.explanation: Yes! Pulling off a banana's yellow outer layer by hand is called peeling.
quests.funFact: This step is one of the easiest ways to prepare a fruit for eating!

quests.instruction: This small citrus fruit peels easier than an orange and tastes a little sweeter too. What is it?
quests.question: Tangerine
quests.hint: This fruit's skin practically falls off with barely any effort.
quests.explanation: Yes! This small, easy-to-peel, sweeter citrus fruit is a tangerine.
quests.funFact: This fruit's loose, easy-to-remove skin is one of its most popular features!

quests.instruction: Grapes still attached to one stem are sold as a bunch, while apples gathered together in a big woven container are carried in a ___. What's the word?
quests.question: Basket
quests.hint: This word names a woven container, not a group still attached to a stem.
quests.explanation: Yes! Apples gathered together in a big woven container are carried in a basket.
quests.funFact: This woven container has been used to gather fruit for thousands of years!

quests.instruction: A ripe peach drips with liquid, while unripe rhubarb has a sharp, pleasant bite. Which word describes the rhubarb's flavor?
quests.question: Tart
quests.hint: This taste is sharp but pleasant, gentler than a fully sour lemon.
quests.explanation: Yes! Rhubarb's sharp, pleasant bite that's gentler than fully sour is called tart.
quests.funFact: Bakers often choose fruit with this milder sharp taste for pies, since it's pleasant, not overpowering!

quests.instruction: Apple seeds and a peach pit are both found in the center of their fruits, but only one is a single hard piece. Which word names that single hard piece?
quests.question: Pit
quests.hint: Count how many there are — this word describes just one, not several.
quests.explanation: Yes! A peach has just one single hard piece in its center, called a pit, unlike an apple's many small seeds.
quests.funFact: This single hard part is exactly why peaches and cherries are both called stone fruits!

quests.instruction: Before baking a pie, Grandma removes the tough middle part of each apple, along with its seeds. What word names that tough, seedy middle part?
quests.question: Core
quests.hint: This word names the center part, not the outer skin.
quests.explanation: Yes! The tough, seedy middle part removed from an apple before baking is called its core.
quests.funFact: A special little tool exists just for removing this part in one quick motion!

quests.instruction: Lucas notices his family's fig tree needs years of patient growing, just like their apple and pear trees nearby. Which category do figs, apples, and pears all share, based on how they grow?
quests.question: Tree Fruit
quests.hint: This category of fruit needs sturdy branches, not a bush or a vine.
quests.explanation: Yes! Figs, apples, and pears, all needing patient growing on sturdy branches, share the tree fruit category.
quests.funFact: Some plants in this fruit category take several years to produce their very first fruit!

quests.instruction: A banana's outer covering comes off with just your fingers, while a coconut's outer covering needs real tools. What's the word for the coconut's tough covering?
quests.question: Husk
quests.hint: This word names a covering tough enough to need a knife or a hammer.
quests.explanation: Yes! A coconut's tough, fibrous outer covering, needing real tools to remove, is called its husk.
quests.funFact: This fibrous part of a coconut can even be turned into rope or mats!

quests.instruction: Dad leaves a hard, green avocado on the counter for two days until it softens. What word describes what happened to the avocado?
quests.question: Ripen
quests.hint: This word describes the natural change from firm to soft over time.
quests.explanation: Yes! An avocado left out for two days until it softens has begun to ripen.
quests.funFact: Placing this fruit inside a paper bag can help speed up this whole process!

quests.instruction: Before a picnic, Marcus slices a whole watermelon into large triangular pieces to share with his friends. Which word names those large triangular pieces?
quests.question: Wedge
quests.hint: This word names a piece shaped like a triangle, wider on one end.
quests.explanation: Yes! Large triangular pieces cut from a whole watermelon are called wedges.
quests.funFact: Cutting a melon this way is a favorite method at summer picnics!

quests.instruction: An orange naturally splits into juicy sections, while a watermelon has a tough outer layer instead. What's the word for one of the orange's juicy sections?
quests.question: Segment
quests.hint: This word names one single natural wedge, not the whole fruit.
quests.explanation: Yes! One of the natural juicy sections an orange splits into is called a segment.
quests.funFact: This natural design makes oranges especially easy to share with friends!

quests.instruction: Before eating a papaya, Diego notices its seeds cluster together in the middle, tasting sharp and unsweet if he tries one. Which word describes that sharp, unsweet taste?
quests.question: Bitter
quests.hint: This taste is often a fruit's way of warning that a part isn't meant to be eaten.
quests.explanation: Yes! The sharp, unsweet taste of a papaya's seeds is called bitter.
quests.funFact: Some seeds and rinds carry this taste to help protect the fruit from being eaten too early!

quests.instruction: At the store, Fatima grabs just a small handful of blueberries to snack on right away, rather than a whole basket. Which word describes that small, one-hand amount?
quests.question: Handful
quests.hint: This word names an amount sized for just one hand, not a whole container.
quests.explanation: Yes! A small, one-hand amount of blueberries grabbed for a quick snack is called a handful.
quests.funFact: Small fruits like these are perfect for grabbing this exact amount as a quick snack!

quests.instruction: Blueberries grow on a low, leafy bush, while watermelons grow low, resting right on the ground. Which word describes where watermelons rest as they grow?
quests.question: Ground
quests.hint: This word describes a spot low enough that you'd bend down, not reach up.
quests.explanation: Yes! Watermelons grow low, resting right on the ground as their vines spread out.
quests.funFact: This low-growing habit means these fruits are picked by bending down, not reaching up!

quests.instruction: Before biting into an orange, Sam peels away its thick skin, then pulls it apart into juicy pieces. What word names each of those juicy pieces?
quests.question: Segment
quests.hint: This word names one single natural piece the orange splits into.
quests.explanation: Yes! Each juicy piece an orange naturally splits into is called a segment.
quests.funFact: This natural design makes oranges especially easy to share with friends!

quests.instruction: A firm green banana left on the counter will slowly turn soft and yellow. Which word describes this natural change?
quests.question: Ripen
quests.hint: This word describes the natural process, not a step you do with your hands.
quests.explanation: Yes! A firm green banana slowly turning soft and yellow describes the process of ripening.
quests.funFact: Some fruits release a natural gas that helps nearby fruit do this even faster!

quests.instruction: Apples and pears grow high on tall branches, while mangoes and pineapples grow in hot, sunny places near the equator. Which category do mangoes and pineapples belong to?
quests.question: Tropical Fruit
quests.hint: This category of fruit almost never survives a cold winter.
quests.explanation: Yes! Mangoes and pineapples, grown in hot, sunny climates, belong to the tropical fruit category.
quests.funFact: This fruit category thrives in warm, humid weather all year round!

quests.instruction: A hard, green banana is called unripe, while one with brown spots and soft golden skin is called ___. What's the word?
quests.question: Ripe
quests.hint: This word describes fruit that's reached its very best, sweetest stage.
quests.explanation: Yes! A banana with brown spots and soft golden skin has reached its best stage, called ripe.
quests.funFact: A fruit at this perfect stage usually tastes its very sweetest!

quests.instruction: Lemons and oranges share a juicy, sectioned inside, while watermelons and cantaloupes grow big and mostly full of water. Which category do watermelons and cantaloupes belong to?
quests.question: Melon
quests.hint: This category of fruit almost always needs two hands and a big knife to cut.
quests.explanation: Yes! Watermelons and cantaloupes, big and mostly full of water, belong to the melon category.
quests.funFact: Fruits in this category are related to cucumbers and squash!

quests.instruction: Before eating an orange, you peel away its skin, and before adding lime juice to guacamole, you must first do what to the lime?
quests.question: Squeeze
quests.hint: This word means pressing a fruit to release its juice, not removing its skin.
quests.explanation: Yes! Before adding lime juice to guacamole, a cook must squeeze the lime to release its juice.
quests.funFact: A splash of this juice also helps keep mashed avocado from turning brown!

quests.instruction: A watermelon's tough green shell is called its rind, while its soft, juicy red inside is called its ___. What's the word?
quests.question: Flesh
quests.hint: This word names the part you actually eat, not the tough part you toss away.
quests.explanation: Yes! A watermelon's soft, juicy red inside, the part you eat, is called its flesh.
quests.funFact: This soft part is usually the biggest portion of a fruit by far!

quests.instruction: Grapes and raisins share the same fruit, one just fresh and one with its water removed. Which category describes the raisin's special preparation?
quests.question: Dried Fruit
quests.hint: This category of fruit has had almost all of its natural water removed.
quests.explanation: Yes! A raisin, with almost all its water removed, belongs to the dried fruit category.
quests.funFact: Removing the water this way lets fruit stay good to eat for months longer!

quests.instruction: A baker might zest a lemon's outer peel for flavor, or squeeze its juice into a recipe. Which word means grating just the fragrant outer peel, not the juice?
quests.question: Zest
quests.hint: This word means grating, not pressing or pulling away by hand.
quests.explanation: Yes! Grating a lemon's fragrant outer peel for flavor, without touching its juice, is called zest.
quests.funFact: This step captures the fragrant oils hiding in a citrus fruit's colorful outer layer!

quests.instruction: This wrinkly brown fruit grows on a desert palm and tastes like natural caramel. What is it?
quests.question: Date
quests.hint: This fruit's home is a hot, sunny desert, not a leafy garden tree.
quests.explanation: Yes! This wrinkly fruit growing on a desert palm with a caramel-like taste is a date.
quests.funFact: This fruit is a favorite sweet treat in many desert regions of the world!

quests.instruction: A whole watermelon is cut into large triangular pieces called wedges, while a whole fruit tray might be cut into thin, flat pieces called ___. What's the word?
quests.question: Slice
quests.hint: This word describes a thin, flat cut, not a wider triangle shape.
quests.explanation: Yes! A thin, flat cut piece of fruit, unlike a wider triangle, is called a slice.
quests.funFact: Cutting fruit into pieces like this makes it much easier to share!

quests.instruction: Grandma keeps a jar of raisins in her pantry, made from grapes that lost nearly all their water. Which word describes fruit prepared that way?
quests.question: Dried Fruit
quests.hint: This word describes fruit that's had nearly every drop of its liquid taken away.
quests.explanation: Yes! Raisins, made from grapes that lost nearly all their water, are an example of dried fruit.
quests.funFact: Removing the water this way lets fruit stay good to eat for much longer!

quests.instruction: Cherries and plums both hide one hard pit, while lemons and oranges are packed with juicy, tangy sections. Which category do lemons and oranges belong to?
quests.question: Citrus Fruit
quests.hint: This category of fruit is famous for being packed with vitamin C.
quests.explanation: Yes! Lemons and oranges, packed with juicy, tangy sections, belong to the citrus fruit category.
quests.funFact: Sailors once carried this fruit category on long voyages to stay healthy!

quests.instruction: Before adding lemon zest to her cookies, Olivia first grates just the yellow outer peel, being careful to avoid the bitter white part underneath. What word names what Olivia just did?
quests.question: Zest
quests.hint: This word means grating a fruit's fragrant outer layer, not squeezing its juice.
quests.explanation: Yes! Grating just a lemon's yellow outer peel for flavor is called zesting.
quests.funFact: Grating too deep into the white part beneath the peel can add an unwanted bitter taste!

quests.instruction: An overripe pear feels squishy in your hand, while a firm nashi pear snaps loudly with each bite. Which word describes the firm pear's texture?
quests.question: Crunchy
quests.hint: This word describes a bite firm enough to push back against your teeth.
quests.explanation: Yes! A firm nashi pear's loud, snapping bite is described as crunchy.
quests.funFact: This firm, snappy bite is one reason apples and pears are such popular lunchbox snacks!

quests.instruction: Apples grow high on the branches of a tall tree, while dates grow high on a tall desert palm. Which word describes what apples grow on?
quests.question: Tree
quests.hint: This word names a tall, woody plant with spreading branches, not a bare trunk.
quests.explanation: Yes! Apples grow high up on the branches of a tall, woody tree.
quests.funFact: Farmers who grow fruit this way often need tall ladders at harvest time!
